title: The ladder of love
hook: Diotima teaches Socrates that love climbs from one beautiful person to beauty itself (Symposium 210–211)

segments.voice: Yesterday, chesed, a word for love. Your line was many words. Did you catch which kind you meant? Today, one more Greek word, and a staircase. Day eight hundred twenty.

A dinner party in Athens, in Plato's Symposium. The guests agree to go easy on the wine and take turns giving speeches in praise of love. When it's Socrates' turn, he does something odd for a famous talker. He doesn't offer his own view. He says a woman taught him what love is, a wise woman from Mantinea named Diotima, and he simply passes on her lesson. What she taught him has a shape, and the shape is a climb.
screen: `A DINNER PARTY IN ATHENS.` → `SOCRATES PASSES IT ON.` → `DIOTIMA OF MANTINEA.`

segments.voice: First, one beautiful person. The Greek word all night is eros, love as longing, love that wants what it doesn't yet have. Diotima says this love often begins with one beautiful person, and the lover is moved to speak beautiful words. Second, beauty in others. Then the lover notices that the beauty in one body is akin to the beauty in another, and the love widens past a single face. Third, beauty of soul. Next comes the beauty of minds and character, then the beauty in good laws and ways of living, then the beauty of knowledge. Fourth, beauty itself. At the top, Diotima says, the lover suddenly sees a beauty that doesn't grow or fade, isn't lovely in one way and ugly in another, and is the source of every beautiful thing below it. Readers call it the ladder of love, because she describes going up as if by steps. It's easy to hear this as climbing away from people, and some readers do hear it that way. Others hear it differently: the first love isn't thrown away, it's the bottom rung, and without it there's no ladder at all. Plato leaves room for both readings. What's plain in the text is the direction. Love, for Diotima, is a reaching, and it keeps reaching past the thing it started with.
screen: `ONE BEAUTIFUL PERSON.` · `BEAUTY IN OTHERS.` · `BEAUTY OF SOUL.` · `BEAUTY ITSELF.` · then, large: `THE LADDER OF LOVE.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes rest on something beautiful near you, or bring one to mind: a face, a line of music, a kind act you once saw, an idea that made you sit up. Stay with it for a few breaths. Then let your attention climb one step. What is it in this that lifts you? Not the thing itself, but its beauty. Notice where that takes you, without forcing it any higher. If nothing comes, stay on the first rung; it's part of the ladder too. The bell holds the time.
Eros. Love as longing, the force in Plato's Symposium that climbs, step by step, from one beautiful person toward beauty itself. Today's word.
Your line: the ladder. Today, when something beautiful stops you, ask what it might be a step toward. Day eight hundred twenty.

howItsDone: Readers of Plato's Symposium, in philosophy classes and in some mystical writing shaped by Plato, discuss Diotima's ascent from the love of one person to the love of beauty itself.

original.note: Greek: love as longing, the love the Symposium's speeches praise; Diotima's ladder is a climb of this love.

trapdoor: what you thought: a ladder of love must mean loving more people.
what it means: Diotima's love climbs from one beautiful person, to beauty in others, in souls, in laws and knowledge, to beauty itself.
what a scholar hears: Socrates credits the teaching to Diotima, and readers still argue whether the climb leaves the first love behind or stands on it.
recall: a blessing for the body's openings

notes: All of Plato is paraphrased (Jowett 1871 is public domain but not on the validator's list); consider adding Jowett to the list so short lines can be quoted.
Order of the ascent (one body, all bodies, souls, laws and practices, knowledge, beauty itself) follows 210a–211c; confirm.
'Readers call it the ladder' and 'as if by steps': Diotima's image of steps is at 211c; confirm.
The two readings (leaving the first love behind vs. standing on it) are described without ranking; confirm fairness.
